title: Bigamy prosecution - why convictions remain rare
p1:
Two marriages. One law. Yet very few people are actually convicted for bigamy.

Why does a case that seems straightforward often become difficult in court?
p2:
Many assume that if someone marries again while the first marriage exists, a conviction automatically follows. But the law requires proof of specific facts, not just suspicion or a relationship outside marriage.

A surprising point: proving the second marriage itself can be the biggest challenge. Courts usually require evidence that all essential marriage ceremonies were properly performed. A simple registration, social media post, or living together may not be enough.
p3:
This is why many complaints fail. The issue is often not whether someone acted unfairly, but whether the legal requirements for a criminal offence have been clearly established.

The practical takeaway: criminal cases depend on evidence, and in bigamy cases, proving the legal validity of both marriages is often the key factor.
conclusion: Do you think bigamy laws are difficult to enforce because of legal requirements, or because many cases are based on facts that are hard to prove?
